lessons.title: Knowing what to write and for whom
lessons.html:
Writing and presenting in the workshop

Equipment service and repair is not only about spanners and grease. You also write job cards, fill in service checklists, order parts, write notes for the next shift and sometimes present information to your team. Others use what you write to decide what to do, so it must be clear and correct.

Common workshop texts

TextPurpose
Job cardRecords the fault, the work done, parts used and hours
Service checklistShows each service step was done
Parts requisitionAsks the store for parts
Handover noteTells the next person what still needs doing
Incident reportRecords an accident or near miss
NoticeTells everyone about a change or a danger

Before you write, ask

  1. Who will read it? The foreman, the store clerk, the farmer, the next mechanic?
  2. Why am I writing? To record, ask, inform or warn?
  3. What do they need to know? List the facts.

Facts to include

Most workshop writing needs these facts:

  • Machine: make, model, serial or fleet number
  • What was wrong (the fault or complaint)
  • What you found when you checked
  • What you did
  • Parts used, with part numbers and quantities
  • Time spent
  • Date, your name and signature

Example: 'Tractor T05, 3 April 2026. Complaint: hydraulics slow. Found: hydraulic filter blocked. Replaced filter (1 x part no. on store sheet). Tested lift, now normal. 1.5 hours. J. Mokoena.'

lessons.title: Writing clearly and neatly
lessons.html:
Making your writing easy to understand

Simple rules

  • Write short sentences.
  • Use the right names for parts and tools.
  • Put things in the order they happened.
  • Write numbers with units: 12 L, 35 Nm, 2.5 hours, R480.
  • Write dates in full, for example 3 April 2026.
  • Write neatly in pen. Use block letters if asked.

Weak and better examples

Weak: 'Fixed the thing on the baler.'

Better: 'Baler B02: replaced broken shear bolt on the pick-up drive. Checked other bolts. Baler working.'

The better one says which machine, what was done and the result.

Filling in forms

  1. Read the whole form before you start.
  2. Fill in every box that applies to you. Write N/A if a box does not apply.
  3. Use the correct format, such as ticking boxes or writing numbers in the right column.
  4. Check spelling of names and part numbers.
  5. Sign and date.

Fixing mistakes

On a job card or checklist, draw one line through a mistake, write the correct information next to it and add your initials. Do not use correction fluid or scribble it out.

Drawings and sketches

Sometimes a sketch explains better than words. Draw a simple picture of where a crack is on a chassis or how hoses are routed. Label the parts and add measurements.

Honest records

Never tick a service step you did not do, such as checking wheel nut torque. A false record can lead to a breakdown or an accident on the farm, and you can be held responsible.

lessons.title: Presenting information to others
lessons.html:
Short presentations at work

Your foreman may ask you to explain something to the team, such as a new safety rule or how a new tool works. This is a short presentation.

Plan the presentation

  1. Decide the main message. What must people remember?
  2. Think about the audience. What do they already know?
  3. Choose two to four main points.
  4. Get things to show: the tool, a part, a picture or a chart.

Structure

  • Beginning: greet the group and say what you will talk about.
  • Middle: explain your main points one by one. Show and demonstrate.
  • End: repeat the most important point and ask for questions.

Delivering

  • Stand where everyone can see and hear you.
  • Speak clearly, not too fast.
  • Look at the people in the group.
  • Use simple words and explain any new word.
  • Move away from noisy machines, or switch them off.

Using visual aids

A flipchart with large letters, a real part, or a picture on a phone or poster helps people understand. Keep words on posters short. Make sure everyone can see.

Making a notice

A notice tells everyone something important. Use a big clear heading, such as 'DANGER: Compressor under repair'. Add a short message, the date and the name of the person to contact. Put it where people will see it, and remove it when it is no longer needed.

Getting feedback

After writing or presenting, ask someone if it was clear. Use their comments to improve next time.

Key points

  • Know who will read your writing and why.
  • Include machine details, the fault, what you found, what you did, parts and time.
  • Write short sentences with units and full dates.
  • Correct mistakes with one line and your initials.
  • Never record work you did not do.
  • Plan presentations with a beginning, middle and end, and show real items.
